title: Gatekeepers, Treasurers, and Officials
summary: The Levitical gatekeepers are organized by family (the Korahites, including the large family of Obed-edom, and the Merarites) and assigned gates by lot. Other Levites are placed over the temple treasuries and the dedicated spoils of war gathered since the days of Samuel. Still others serve as officers and judges and oversee the affairs of Israel on both sides of the Jordan.
story: This chapter continues the organization of the temple that began in chapter 23: Levites, then priests (24), then musicians (25), and now gatekeepers, treasurers, and officials. Chapter 27 will finish with the army and civil administration. By this point the Chronicler has shown that every part of temple service, from the altar to the doors, is in place before Solomon lays a stone. The chapter also looks back: the treasury holds gifts dedicated by Samuel, Saul, Abner, Joab, and David, gathering Israel's history into the house of God.
historical:
The gatekeepers came from two Levitical families: the Korahites, of the Kohathite clan (the family associated with the sons of Korah in the Psalms), and the Merarites. The Asaph named in verse 1 is probably not the musician of chapter 25, who was a Gershonite; many take him to be the Korahite Ebiasaph named in 1 Chronicles 9:19 and 6:37. Obed-edom is presumably the man in whose house the ark rested for three months (13:14), where the LORD blessed his household. Verse 5 echoes that: for God had blessed Obed-edom, and his family of sixty-two capable men is the evidence.

Verse 31 dates the search of the Hebronite records to the fortieth year of David's reign, his last year, which fits the setting of these chapters at the end of his life. Jazer in Gilead lay east of the Jordan. The appointment of Levites over the eastern tribes (Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh) and over the west shows religious and royal administration working together across the kingdom. Gatekeepers remained an important order after the exile; Ezra 2:42 lists them among the returning exiles, and 1 Chronicles 9 describes their duties.
cultural:
Gatekeepers were more than doormen. They controlled access to the temple precincts, guarded against the unclean or unauthorized entering, protected the storerooms and treasuries, and in some settings maintained order. The chapter assigns them to the four sides: east, north, south, and west, with the Shallecheth Gate on the ascending highway (a gate named only here), and posts guards at every watch. The east gate faced the temple's entrance and received the largest guard.

In the ancient world, temples functioned as treasuries as well as places of worship. Gifts and spoils dedicated to a god were stored there, and the temple's wealth was guarded carefully. Israel dedicated spoils of war to the LORD (as David did in 18:11), and verse 27 says some plunder went to repair the house of the LORD. The Levites who were officers and judges (verse 29) served outside the temple, helping administer justice in the land, a role that 2 Chronicles 19:8-11 also describes.
literary: The chapter has three parts: gatekeepers (verses 1-19), treasurers (verses 20-28), and outside officials (verses 29-32). Each is organized by family, following the pattern of chapters 23 to 25. The recurring phrase is capable men, or men of strength (verses 6-9, 30-32), which marks this list as a roster of trustworthy, able people. The notes about Zechariah as a wise counselor (verse 14) and Shimri appointed first though not the firstborn (verse 10) show attention to character and ability as well as descent. The long list of those who dedicated treasure (verse 28), from Samuel the seer to Joab, gives the chapter a sense of history converging on the temple.

outline.t: The treasuries and the dedicated gifts
Officers and judges for Israel's affairs

doctrines.note: The gatekeepers guarded the approach to God's house. Their work expressed the truth that God's presence is holy and must be approached rightly, the lesson of chapters 13 and 15.

God had blessed Obed-edom (verse 5). The man who sheltered the ark in a dangerous season now has a large family serving at the temple's doors. Faithfulness in one moment bears fruit across generations.

Worship depends on people with differing gifts: guards, treasurers, administrators, and judges, all counted as service to the LORD and to the king. The chapter honors practical and administrative work as part of God's house.

words.note: Shaar, gate. In the ancient world the gate was a place of access, defense, and often judgment. Here the temple gates are assigned by lot to the families that guard them (verses 13-16). Psalm 84:10 celebrates even the lowly place of a doorkeeper in God's house.

Otsar, treasury or storehouse. The temple treasuries held gifts and dedicated spoils (verses 20-26). The word can also mean the treasure itself. The Levites' care of it was a trust, since what was dedicated belonged to God.

Chayil, strength, ability, or worth. It is used of military strength, wealth, and excellence of character (Proverbs 31:10 uses it for the woman of noble character). Here the capable men are those with strength and ability for the work.

Qadash, here to dedicate. Things dedicated by King David, the commanders, Samuel, Saul, Abner, and Joab were set apart as holy (verses 26-28). Dedication moved them from ordinary use to God's possession.

christ: The New Testament uses the image of the gate or door for Christ himself: in John 10 Jesus calls himself the gate for the sheep and says that whoever enters through him will be saved (John 10:7-9). Where Levitical gatekeepers guarded access to a holy place, Christ is the way of access to God (Ephesians 2:18). The treasure dedicated to the LORD also finds an echo in Jesus' teaching about storing up treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:19-21). These connections are thematic, drawn by the wider biblical story rather than predicted by this chapter.
questions: Obed-edom sheltered the ark when others were afraid, and God blessed his family for generations. What small acts of faithfulness might bear fruit you'll never see?
The gatekeepers, treasurers, and administrators were all serving God. Which unnoticed roles in your community deserve more honor?
The treasury held gifts from Samuel, Saul, Abner, Joab, and David, people with very mixed stories. What does it mean that God's house is built from the gifts of imperfect people?
